structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father's advice to reserve judgment, which shaped his role as a confidant and led to his unique admiration for Gatsby, whom he sees as possessing an extraordinary gift for hope. In spring 1922, Nick moves alone to West Egg, renting a modest bungalow between two grand estates, and feels a sense of belonging after helping a stranger locate the village. That same evening, he drives by car to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a physically imposing Yale acquaintance, where he meets Jordan Baker, a detached and aloof woman. During dinner, Tom aggressively recites racist pseudoscience from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, a phone call from his mistress in New York disrupts the meal, and Daisy, visibly shaken, confesses to Nick her cynical wish that their daughter be a 'beautiful little fool.' As Nick departs, he pauses in his yard at West Egg under a bright summer night, where he observes Gatsby standing alone on the lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light across the bay before vanishing into the darkness.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway accompanies Tom Buchanan by train from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where Tom forcibly pulls him from the train to meet Myrtle Wilson, wife of George Wilson, at his run-down garage; Myrtle joins them on the train, traveling separately to maintain appearances, and purchases a dog, Town Tattle magazine, perfume, and cold cream at the station before boarding a lavender taxicab to her rented apartment on 158th Street, where she hosts a chaotic gathering with her sister Catherine and the McKees, during which she drinks heavily, changes into a chiffon dress, adopts an exaggerated socialite demeanor, and falsely claims Daisy Buchanan is a Catholic who opposes divorce; tensions erupt when Myrtle drunkenly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose, after which blood stains the bathroom floor and guests flee, leaving Nick exhausted and alone in Pennsylvania Station at dawn.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway receiving a formal invitation to Jay Gatsby’s lavish Saturday evening party at his West Egg mansion, where guests arrive by automobile and Rolls-Royce from New York, filling the garden with orchestras, cocktails, and extravagant displays including weekly deliveries of five crates of fruit and a bar stocked with forgotten cordials. Amid wild rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick Carraway meets Jordan Baker, explores the library where a drunken guest marvels at the authenticity of Gatsby’s real books, and encounters a war veteran who offers him a hydroplane ride—yet still has not seen Gatsby. Later, after consuming champagne and witnessing chaotic scenes—including a weeping chorus girl, marital fights, and a coupé crashing into a wall with Owl Eyes claiming he wasn’t driving—Nick Carraway finally meets Gatsby, who reveals himself as a calm, reassuring man with precise diction, invites him for a hydroplane ride the next morning, and is abruptly called away by a phone call from Chicago. As the party dissolves into silence, Nick Carraway leaves to find Gatsby standing alone on the porch under the moon, formally bidding farewell. In reflection, Nick Carraway recalls his ordinary daily life in New York: commuting on foot to the Probity Trust, lunches with clerks, studying investments at the Yale Club, and a brief romance that ended when a girl from Jersey City went on vacation; he re-encounters Jordan Baker in midsummer, disillusioned by her dishonesty—lying about damaging a borrowed car and cheating in a golf tournament—and recognizes his lingering emotional entanglement with a woman back home, symbolized by her perspiration-moustache while playing tennis, before resolving to end their correspondence.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion erupts into chaotic revelry as guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York arrive by car, mingling amid cocktails and flowers while spreading absurd rumors about his origins—including ties to Von Hindenburg and the devil—many of whom, like Snell and Klipspringer, are known for drunkenness or permanent presence, yet remain utterly ignorant of Gatsby himself. Later that July, Gatsby picks up Nick Carraway in his cream-colored car with nickel accents and a three-noted horn, revealing a meticulously crafted but dubious backstory of Oxford education, European aristocracy, and wartime heroism, backed by a Montenegrin medal and an Oxford photograph, before hinting at a request involving Jordan Baker. At noon in a cellar on Forty-second Street, Nick Carraway dines with Gatsby and Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque figure with human molar cuff buttons, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and shockingly reveals Gatsby fixed the 1919 World Series, before Gatsby abruptly departs upon spotting Tom Buchanan. Flashing back to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, a moment of intense romance that preceded Daisy’s near-elopement with him and her eventual marriage to Tom Buchanan, marked by a drunken wedding day where she sobbed over a letter and a three-hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar pearl necklace. After leaving the Plaza Hotel, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy and now seeks a tea invitation to reunite with her unknowingly, prompting Nick Carraway to become emotionally drawn to Jordan as they ride through Central Park in a victoria at twilight, culminating in his reflection: 'There are only the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, and the tired.'

structure.title: V
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick returning to his modest West Egg home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit by flickering lights, no party in progress—only the wind stirring the night. Gatsby nervously invites Nick to Coney Island or a swim, but Nick declines, instead offering to arrange a tea with Daisy; Gatsby then awkwardly probes Nick’s income and offers a secretive side business, which Nick refuses. The next morning, rain forces Gatsby to send a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn, and he arrives early in a white suit, visibly anxious, obsessing over tea preparations. When Daisy arrives by large open car with chauffeur Ferdie, Gatsby is so overwhelmed he nearly knocks over a clock; after an excruciatingly awkward reunion, Nick steps away and returns to find Daisy crying and Gatsby radiating quiet joy, the two now at ease. Gatsby invites Daisy to tour his mansion, walking with her along the road rather than the Sound, entering through the big postern as she admires the feudal silhouette, gardens filled with jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate. Inside, they wander through opulent, empty rooms—Marie Antoinette music-rooms, Restoration Salons, period bedrooms—where Nick hears what he believes is the owl-eyed man’s ghostly laughter; Gatsby shows Daisy his extensive wardrobe of luxurious shirts, which overwhelms her to the point of uncontrollable weeping as she buries her face in the silk and linen. After the rain clears, Gatsby points out the diminished green light at Daisy’s dock, shows Nick a photograph of Mr. Dan Cody and a youthful picture of himself in yachting gear, and reveals clippings about Daisy; their moment is interrupted by a phone call about a misplaced Detroit contact. Daisy marvels at pink clouds over the Sound, whispering a tender fantasy of enclosing Gatsby in one. Gatsby calls Klipspringer to play piano, who reluctantly performs 'The Love Nest' and 'In the Morning, In the Evening'; as Nick prepares to leave, he finds Gatsby and Daisy lost in each other, emotionally reconnected yet distant from the world, Gatsby’s face clouded by doubt as he clutches Daisy’s hand, utterly absorbed in her voice.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion one morning, drawn by wild rumors—such as the myth that Gatsby lives in a moving boat disguised as a house—reflecting his rising notoriety; the narrative then traces Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, changed his name after encountering Dan Cody’s yacht on Lake Superior, where he worked as a clam-digger and fisherman while dreaming of wealth, before being taken aboard as a protege for five years of seafaring adventures that shaped his identity, though he inherited nothing from Cody’s estate, which was claimed entirely by Ella Kaye. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, offers drinks and supper invitations, but they coldly refuse, with Sloane subtly blocking Gatsby when he attempts to follow them in his car after their departure. Later that evening, Tom and Daisy attend Gatsby’s party, where Daisy becomes visibly unsettled by the chaos of West Egg and grows distant after a brief private moment with Gatsby, while Tom suspects Gatsby is a bootlegger and Daisy defends him with a fabricated story about owning drugstores; afterward, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway his despair that Daisy did not enjoy the evening and his obsessive belief that he can recreate the past by having her tell Tom she never loved him, so they can return to Louisville and restart their relationship as if five years had never passed, standing alone in the garden amid discarded party debris with his eyes fixed on the horizon.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans' house to find Gatsby waiting, having dismissed his original servants and replaced them with Wolfsheim’s relatives to conceal Daisy’s afternoon visits; during a stifling luncheon, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby while Tom watches with growing suspicion, leading Tom to challenge Gatsby’s claim of being an Oxford man and insist they all go to town. The group splits into two cars—Tom takes Gatsby’s coupé with Daisy, while Nick, Jordan, and Gatsby drive in Gatsby’s car—to stop at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes, where a sickly Wilson reveals his desperation to move West and Tom discloses his plan to take Myrtle away, causing Myrtle to peer from the window and mistake Jordan for Tom’s wife. The group then travels to the Plaza Hotel in New York, where a volatile argument erupts: Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim, while Gatsby demands Daisy declare she never loved Tom; overwhelmed, Daisy confesses she once loved both men, shattering Gatsby’s dream, and Tom orders them to leave together in Gatsby’s car. Later, Myrtle Wilson rushes out of the garage and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that flees; Michaelis witnesses the scene and describes the car as light green, while witnesses confirm its speed at 50–60 mph. Tom and Nick arrive at the garage to find Myrtle’s body, and Tom falsely insists his own blue car is not the killer, calming Wilson before driving away in tears. Finally, Nick waits outside the Buchanan house, where Gatsby emerges to reveal Daisy was driving the fatal car and insists he will take the blame; through a pantry window, Nick sees Daisy and Tom quietly sharing chicken and ale, already reconciled, as Gatsby stands vigil in the moonlight, unaware the danger has passed.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: On the dawn after Daisy’s brief appearance at her window, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion and finds him dejected, having waited all night for her signal; they search the dusty, neglected house for cigarettes before sitting on the terrace as Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the belief that Daisy never truly loved Tom and will choose him. Gatsby recounts his youth with Dan Cody and his first encounter with Daisy, revealing how her wealth and lifestyle became an ideal he pursued by deception, and later describes his painful return to Louisville on his last army pay, walking their shared streets and riding away on a hot day-coach, realizing he had lost the 'freshest and the best' part of his life. On the same morning, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, instructs the butler to bring any calls to the pool, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage with the chauffeur’s help, and forbids use of the damaged open car; he carries the mattress alone toward the pool, while the butler waits awake until dawn, still hoping for Daisy’s call. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and convinced his wife Myrtle was murdered by the driver of a yellow car, travels on foot from his garage to Port Roosevelt and then Gad’s Hill, buying a sandwich and coffee, vanishes for three hours before appearing in West Egg and asking for Gatsby’s house—revealing he now knows Gatsby’s name. At two o’clock, gunfire is heard; Nick Carraway rushes to the mansion with the butler, chauffeur, and gardener to find Gatsby’s body floating face-down on the mattress in the pool, and moments later discovers Wilson’s body in the grass, completing the tragedy. In a parallel thread, Nick Carraway wakes in his city office, exhausted, after receiving a cold, abrupt call from Jordan Baker—who accuses him of unfriendliness and plans to travel by car to Southampton—and fails to reach Gatsby’s house after four attempts due to a long-distance call from Detroit; he marks the 3:50 train on his timetable and sits in silence.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: After Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage the chaotic aftermath as police, photographers, and curious onlookers swarm the mansion, while media and Catherine’s denial reduce Wilson’s actions to the tragedy of a 'madman.' Despite desperate attempts to contact Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim—via phone, letter, and in-person visits—no one responds except Wolfsheim’s cold, evasive note citing 'important business.' On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly frail and emotionally shattered, bundled in a cheap ulster; he is awed by the mansion and shares a childhood book with Gatsby’s self-improvement schedule, revealing the depth of his son’s ambition. The funeral, held at Gatsby’s house, draws only the Lutheran minister and Gatz, as Klipspringer calls to request his tennis shoes be mailed and Wolfsheim refuses to attend, claiming he avoids being 'mixed up' in deaths. In a heavy drizzle, a procession of three cars—motor hearse, limousine carrying Gatz, the minister, and Nick Carraway, followed by Gatsby’s station wagon with servants and the postman—travels to the cemetery, where the owl-eyed man, last seen marveling at Gatsby’s books, appears unexpectedly, wiping rain from his glasses to view the grave and murmuring 'Amen to that' after hearing 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on,' then lamenting, 'The poor son-of-a-bitch.' Before leaving the East, Nick Carraway meets Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man; their bitter exchange ends with his admission that at thirty, he no longer lies to himself about honor. He later encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told George Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary and emotionally manipulating Nick Carraway with a story of crying over dog biscuits; Nick shakes Tom’s hand, seeing him as a child, before watching Tom enter a jewelry store to buy a pearl necklace or cuff buttons. In his final walk to Gatsby’s empty house, Nick Carraway erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps and wanders to the beach, reflecting on Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light and concluding with the metaphor of boats beaten back by a current into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, Long Island, seeking opportunity in the bond business and renting a modest home next to the lavish mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—a wealthy, arrogant Yale alumnus—Nick is introduced to the opulent yet morally hollow world of East Egg’s old money elite. He also meets Jordan Baker, a detached and dishonest golfer, who later reveals that Gatsby’s fortune and mansion were acquired solely to be near Daisy, his lost love from five years prior. Gatsby, who throws extravagant parties attended by strangers who know nothing of him, cautiously draws Nick into his orbit, confiding in him a carefully constructed but fabricated past of Oxford, European aristocracy, and wartime heroism, while secretly hoping Nick will arrange a reunion with Daisy.

Nick agrees to facilitate a tea between Gatsby and Daisy, which reignites their romance and culminates in Gatsby’s belief that he can erase the past and recreate their lost love. As their affair deepens, tensions rise between Gatsby and Tom, who grows suspicious of Gatsby’s wealth and origins. During a sweltering afternoon in New York, the group confronts each other at the Plaza Hotel, where Tom exposes Gatsby’s ties to bootlegging through Meyer Wolfsheim and forces Daisy to admit she once loved both men—shattering Gatsby’s idealized vision. In the aftermath, Daisy, driving Gatsby’s yellow car, accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, who mistakes the car for Tom’s. Tom manipulates George Wilson, Myrtle’s grief-stricken husband, into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, setting in motion a chain of violence.

After the accident, Gatsby waits hopelessly by his pool for a call from Daisy, clinging to the fantasy that she will leave Tom. Meanwhile, George Wilson, misled by Tom, tracks Gatsby to his mansion and shoots him dead before taking his own life. Nick, left to organize Gatsby’s funeral, finds himself utterly alone: Daisy and Tom vanish without a word, Wolfsheim refuses to attend, and even Jordan Baker coldly ends their relationship. Only Gatsby’s impoverished father arrives, proud of his son’s ambition, revealed through a childhood book filled with self-improvement goals. As Nick reflects on the emptiness of the East and the corruption beneath its glittering surface, he concludes that Gatsby’s tragedy was not just in his death, but in his unwavering belief in a dream that could never be reclaimed—a dream embodied by the green light across the bay, forever out of reach, as all dreams are, beaten back by the relentless tide of time.
